name: Executive order of July 21, 1874 restoring to market the part of the White Mountain reservation east of 109° 30' W.
nations: Cibecue and Southern Tonto Apache groups (Western Apache, as named in Docket 22-D)
promises: Not a treaty: a presidential order. It restored to market the part of the White Mountain reservation lying east of 109° 30' west longitude (Royce p. 876, area 573).

breaches.what: The Indian Claims Commission concluded that by the executive orders of August 5, 1873, July 21, 1874, April 27, 1876, January 26, 1877, March 31, 1877 and December 22, 1902 the United States successively extinguished, without paying compensation, Western Apache Indian title to lands inside the enlarged White Mountain reservation, as of the dates of the orders. The order of July 21, 1874 is one of the orders it named.

breaches.what: In its opinion the Commission held that by successively diminishing the enlarged White Mountain reservation by these orders the United States wrongfully took additional Western Apache aboriginal title lands, as described in the orders, as of the orders' dates, and ordered the acreage and value of each excluded tract determined.

landTaken: Royce area 573: the White Mountain reservation east of 109° 30' west longitude. The Commission did not reach the acreage because the claim was settled.
compensation: None at the time. The Western Apache claim (Docket 22-D) was compromised for $4,900,000 in 1972, for all the Western Apache lands taken.
today: The Fort Apache (White Mountain) and San Carlos reservations remain.

plain.promised: Not a treaty: a presidential order. It cut the land east of 109° 30' west longitude out of the White Mountain reservation and opened it to market.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission found in 1969 that by this order and others the United States took Western Apache land inside the reservation without paying for it.
plain.today: Counted once with the 1871 reservation orders. The Western Apache claim was settled for $4,900,000 in 1972.
